lead: CompTIA's Linux admin cert. It proves you can run Linux servers from the command line: storage, networking, users, systemd services, containers, hardening, scripting and troubleshooting. Most servers, cloud workloads and security tools run on Linux, and unlike the LPI certs, Linux+ is on the DoD 8140 matrix.

v8.label: V8
v8.note: The only version you can take now: the old XK0-005 (V7) retired in English on Jan 13, 2026. CompTIA estimates V8 retires around 2028. It splits Services and User Management into its own domain and adds Python, Git, Ansible-style automation and responsible AI use. CompTIA recommends about 12 months of hands-on Linux server work, plus A+ and Network+ level knowledge.
v8.onote: Official objective titles from CompTIA's XK0-006 objectives PDF (document version 5.0). The line under each is a plain-language summary of its bullet list, not the full list.

domains.name: System Management
obj: Explain basic Linux concepts

The boot process (bootloader, kernel, initrd), the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, server architectures, distributions, graphical desktops (X and Wayland) and software licenses: open source, free, proprietary and copyleft.
Summarize Linux device management concepts and tools
Kernel modules (lsmod, modinfo, insmod, modprobe, depmod), device management, initrd and custom hardware.
Given a scenario, manage storage in a Linux system
Partitions, filesystems, LVM (physical volumes, volume groups, logical volumes), RAID, mounted and network storage (NFS, SMB) and inodes.
Given a scenario, manage network services and configurations on a Linux server
/etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf and /etc/nsswitch.conf, NetworkManager (nmcli), Netplan and tools like ip, ss, dig, ping, traceroute and tcpdump.
Given a scenario, manage a Linux system using common shell operations
Environment variables (PATH, HOME, PS1), shell config files, redirection and pipes, text tools (grep, sed, awk, cut, sort, tee, xargs) and the vi and nano editors.
Given a scenario, perform backup and restore operations for a Linux server
Archives (tar, cpio), compression (gzip, bzip2, xz) and other copy and backup tools.
Summarize virtualization on Linux systems
Hypervisors (KVM, QEMU), VM operations, bare metal vs VMs, virtual network types (NAT, bridged, routed, open) and tools like libvirt, virsh and virt-manager.

domains.name: Services and User Management
obj: Given a scenario, manage files and directories on a Linux system
File utilities (cp, mv, find, ln, diff, file, locate and more), hard vs symbolic links, and the device types in /dev.
Given a scenario, perform local account management in a Linux environment
Add, modify, lock, expire, list and delete accounts; /etc/skel templates; /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group; user vs system vs service accounts.
Given a scenario, manage processes and jobs in a Linux environment
Process IDs and states, priority (nice, renice), limits (ulimit), job control (jobs, bg, fg, kill) and scheduling with cron, at and systemd timers.
Given a scenario, configure and manage software in a Linux environment
Install, update and remove packages (apt, dnf, rpm, dpkg), repositories and exclusions, update-alternatives, sandboxed apps (snap, flatpak) and basic configs for common services.
Given a scenario, manage Linux using systemd
Unit types (service, timer, socket, mount, target), systemctl, journalctl and other systemd tools, and unit states: start, stop, enable, disable, mask.
Given a scenario, manage applications in a container on a Linux server
Runtimes (Docker, Podman), image and container operations, volumes, container networks, and privileged vs unprivileged containers.

domains.name: Security
obj: Given a scenario, apply operating system (OS) hardening techniques on a Linux system

sudo and privilege escalation, file attributes, permissions and ACLs, SELinux and AppArmor, secure SSH, dropping unsecure services like Telnet and FTP, removing unneeded SUID bits, disabling unused filesystems and Secure Boot.
Summarize authorization, authentication, and accounting methods
Polkit, PAM, SSSD and Winbind, LDAP, Kerberos, Samba, logging and system auditing.
Given a scenario, configure and implement firewalls on a Linux system
firewalld, ufw, nftables, iptables, ipset and Netfilter, address translation, stateful vs stateless rules and IP forwarding.
Explain account hardening techniques and best practices
Password rules, MFA, checking breach lists, restricted shells, locking accounts after failed logins and not running as root.
Explain cryptographic concepts and technologies in a Linux environment
Protecting data at rest and in transit, hashing, removing weak algorithms, certificate management and why to avoid self-signed certificates.
Explain the importance of compliance and audit procedures
Detection and response, vulnerability scanning, standards and audits, file integrity, secure data destruction, the software supply chain and login banners.

domains.name: Automation, Orchestration, and Scripting
obj: Given a scenario, perform automated tasks using shell scripting
Expansion, functions, IFS/OFS, if and case, loops, the #! line, comparisons and test, regular expressions and variables.
Summarize Python basics used for Linux system administration
Virtual environments, built-in modules, installing dependencies, Python fundamentals and PEP 8 style.
Given a scenario, implement version control using Git
clone, add, commit, branch, checkout, merge, rebase, pull, push, fetch, stash, tag, reset, log, diff and .gitignore.
Summarize best practices and responsible uses of artificial intelligence (AI)
Common use cases, best practices (check what AI writes before you run it) and prompt engineering.
Summarize the use cases and techniques of automation and orchestration in a Linux environment
Infrastructure as code (tools like Ansible, Puppet and OpenTofu), unattended deployment, CI/CD and deployment orchestration.

domains.name: Troubleshooting
obj: Given a scenario, analyze and troubleshoot hardware, storage, and Linux OS issues
Common issues like boot failures, full disks, running out of inodes, filesystem errors and missing devices.
Given a scenario, analyze and troubleshoot networking issues on a Linux system
Common issues like a down interface, a wrong address or route, DNS failures and blocked ports.
Given a scenario, analyze and troubleshoot security issues on a Linux system
Common issues like SELinux denials, wrong permissions or ownership, failed logins and certificate problems.
Given a scenario, analyze and troubleshoot performance issues
Common symptoms like high CPU, memory or swap use, slow disks (I/O wait), high load and runaway processes.
Summarize monitoring concepts and configurations in a Linux system
Service monitoring, how monitoring data is collected, and monitoring configurations.

extras.title: Where things live
rows: System and service settings: sshd_config, fstab, passwd, hosts.
auth.log or secure, messages or syslog, audit/audit.log. Where SOC work starts.
One folder per user. Root's is /root.
The kernel, initrd and bootloader config.
Not real files: process and system details like /proc/cpuinfo.
Anyone can write; the sticky bit stops users deleting each other's files.

extras.title: Permissions at a glance
rows: Add them per group: 7 = rwx, 6 = rw-, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--.
Owner does anything; everyone else can read and run. Scripts, folders.
Owner edits, group reads, others get nothing. Config with secrets.
Runs as the file's owner (often root). Audit every one: find / -perm -4000.
Anyone writes, only the owner deletes. /tmp.

extras.title: systemd in one card
rows: Running or not, recent log lines, and the unit file path.
Change it now. Gone after a reboot unless it's enabled.
Start at every boot and start it right away.
Nobody can start it, not even by hand or as a dependency.
Run after you change a unit file, so systemd rereads it.
This unit's logs since the last boot. Add -p err for errors only, -f to follow.

extras.title: A service won't start
extras.sub: 5.0 · a method that works on the exam and at work
rows: systemctl status <name>: read the error and the last log lines.
journalctl -u <name> -b: read the full log since boot.
Test the config file (for example nginx -t or sshd -t).
ss -tlnp: is another program already on the port?
Check permissions and ownership on the files it needs.
On SELinux systems, check for denials (ausearch -m avc) and labels (ls -Z).
Fix one thing, restart, check status again, then enable it if it should survive a reboot.

method: Use the five domains above as your checklist. System Management and Troubleshooting are almost half the exam.
Run Linux every day. WSL on your own laptop or a free VirtualBox VM is enough. Use one Debian-family and one RHEL-family distro, because the exam uses both.
Break your own lab on purpose: fill a disk, stop a service, block a port, mislabel a file under SELinux. Then fix it with the tools in 5.0.
Flashcards for paths, permission numbers, systemctl and journalctl options, and which package tool goes with which distro.
Timed practice exams with PBQs. Review every miss. A common target is 85%+ twice in a row before you book.
tips: They often come first and eat time. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.
apt and dpkg on Debian and Ubuntu; dnf and rpm on RHEL and Rocky. Many questions hinge on which one fits.
Many questions show command output. Find the one line that matters (100% in df -i, wa in top, denied in the audit log) before you look at the answers.
There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so always pick something.

quiz.q: The /data logical volume (ext4) is full. Its volume group has 20 GB free. Which command adds 10 GB AND grows the filesystem in one step, without unmounting?
o: lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vg0/data
Right. -L +10G grows the logical volume and -r resizes the filesystem on it right after. ext4 can grow while mounted.
lvcreate -L 10G -n data vg0
lvcreate makes a new, separate logical volume. It doesn't grow the existing one.
resize2fs /dev/vg0/data
resize2fs grows the filesystem, but the volume under it is still the same size, so there's no room to grow into yet.
pvcreate /dev/sdc
pvcreate prepares a new disk for LVM. The volume group already has free space, so you don't need a new disk.

quiz.q: An app on a server keeps connecting to a decommissioned database at 10.1.4.20. dig shows db.unit.example resolving to the new address, 10.1.4.55. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: An old entry for db.unit.example in /etc/hosts
Right. dig asks DNS directly, but most apps resolve names through /etc/nsswitch.conf, where "files" (/etc/hosts) is usually checked before DNS.
The DNS server is caching the old record
dig already returns the new address from DNS, so DNS isn't the problem.
A wrong default gateway
A bad gateway causes timeouts, not a connection to a specific old IP address.
NetworkManager needs a restart
Restarting the network doesn't change which IP a name resolves to. The hosts file wins either way.

quiz.q: A nightly script must add BOTH its normal output and its errors to the same log file, keeping earlier nights' entries. Which line is correct?
o: /opt/nightly.sh >> /var/log/nightly.log 2>&1
Right. >> appends, and 2>&1 then sends errors (stream 2) to wherever output (stream 1) already goes: the log.
/opt/nightly.sh 2>&1 >> /var/log/nightly.log
Order matters. 2>&1 runs first, while stdout still points at the terminal, so errors go to the screen and only normal output reaches the log.
/opt/nightly.sh > /var/log/nightly.log 2>&1
This catches both streams, but a single > overwrites the file every night.
/opt/nightly.sh | tee -a /var/log/nightly.log
A pipe carries only stdout. Errors skip tee and never reach the log.

quiz.q: A member transfers out tomorrow. Their files must stay for their replacement, but they must not be able to log in starting now. What is the BEST action?
o: Lock and expire the account (usermod -L and chage -E 0)
Right. Locking blocks the password and expiring the account also blocks key-based logins, while the home folder and files stay put.
userdel -r jdoe
-r deletes the home folder and mail spool, so the files the replacement needs are gone.
passwd -d jdoe
That removes the password entirely. Depending on PAM settings, that can allow a login with no password at all.
Remove jdoe from every group in /etc/group
They lose group access, but they can still log in with their own account.

quiz.q: nginx starts fine with systemctl start, but it's down again every time the server reboots. Which command fixes this?
o: systemctl enable --now nginx
Right. enable makes it start at every boot, and --now starts it right away too.
systemctl restart nginx
Restart only affects the running service. It still won't start after the next reboot.
systemctl mask nginx
mask does the opposite: it blocks the service from starting at all.
systemctl daemon-reload
daemon-reload rereads unit files after you edit them. It doesn't make anything start at boot.

quiz.q: A team runs a database in a container. Every time they pull a new image and recreate the container, all the data disappears. What should they do?
o: Store the data in a named volume mounted into the container
Right. A volume lives outside the container's writable layer, so it survives when the container is deleted and recreated.
Run the container with --privileged
Privileged mode gives the container broad access to the host. It does nothing to keep data, and it's a security risk.
Publish the database port with -p
Publishing a port controls network access, not where data is stored.
Commit the container to a new image after each change
Baking data into images is slow, fragile and mixes data with code. Volumes are the right tool.

quiz.q: A hardening review finds this file. The tool doesn't need root rights to work. What does the s mean, and what is the right fix?
o: SUID: anyone who runs it runs it as root. Remove it with chmod u-s
Right. SUID programs owned by root are a favorite privilege escalation path. If it isn't needed, take it off.
Sticky bit: only root can delete it. Leave it
The sticky bit shows as t in the others' execute spot and is for folders like /tmp. This s is in the owner's execute spot.
SGID: it runs with the root group. Fix it with chmod g-s
SGID would show s in the group's execute spot. Here the group part is r-x.
Swap-enabled: it can page to disk. Fix it with chattr -s
There is no swap permission. s in the owner's execute spot means SUID.

quiz.q: On a RHEL-family server that uses firewalld, web users must reach HTTPS, and the rule must survive a reboot. What should you run?
o: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https, then firewall-cmd --reload
Right. --permanent writes the rule to the saved config, and --reload loads that config into the running firewall.
firewall-cmd --add-service=https
This works right now, but it isn't saved. It's gone after a reload or reboot.
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
Writing raw rules behind firewalld's back isn't saved, and firewalld can wipe it on its next reload.
ufw allow 443/tcp
ufw is a different firewall front end, usually on Ubuntu. It isn't what's managing this server.

quiz.q: Which sshd_config settings BEST harden SSH on a server that every admin reaches with their own key?
o: PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no
Right. Admins log in as themselves and use sudo, which leaves a trail, and with passwords off, password guessing can't work.
Port 2222 and PermitRootLogin yes
A new port cuts down noise in the logs but isn't real protection, and allowing root logins makes things worse.
PasswordAuthentication yes and MaxAuthTries 10
This keeps passwords on and gives attackers more guesses per connection.
Protocol 1 and X11Forwarding yes
SSH protocol 1 is broken and long gone, and X11 forwarding adds attack surface you don't need.

quiz.q: Today's auth.log has 3 lines that contain "Failed password". What does this script print?
quiz.code:
#!/bin/bash
count=$(grep -c "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log)
if [ "$count" -gt 5 ]; then
  echo "ALERT: $count failed logins"
fi
o: Nothing
Right. grep -c counts matching lines (3), and 3 isn't greater than 5, so the if block never runs.
ALERT: 3 failed logins
That only prints when the count is greater than 5.
ALERT: 5 failed logins
5 is the threshold in the test, not the count. The variable holds 3.
An error, because -gt can't compare text
$count holds the number 3, and -gt compares integers, so the test runs fine.

quiz.q: You're halfway through editing a script on a feature branch when you have to fix an urgent bug on main. You don't want to commit half-done work. What should you run FIRST?
o: git stash
Right. stash shelves your uncommitted changes so you can switch branches. git stash pop brings them back later.
git reset --hard
That throws your uncommitted changes away for good.
git commit --amend
That rewrites your last commit with the half-done work, which is exactly what you wanted to avoid.
git rebase main
Rebasing moves your branch's commits. It doesn't deal with uncommitted edits, and Git won't rebase with a dirty tree.

quiz.q: You run the same Ansible playbook against a server twice. The first run makes 12 changes; the second run reports 0 changes. Which property does this show?
o: Idempotency
Right. An idempotent task describes the end state, so running it again on a server that's already there changes nothing.
Immutability
Immutable infrastructure means replacing servers instead of changing them. The playbook changed this server in place.
A pull-based model
Ansible pushes from a control node. Pull vs push is about who starts the run, not repeat runs.
Continuous deployment
CD is about automatically releasing changes through a pipeline, not about repeat runs of one playbook.

quiz.q: A spool job fails with an error, but there seems to be plenty of space. What is the cause?
quiz.code:
$ touch /var/spool/app/job.tmp
touch: cannot touch 'job.tmp': No space left on device
$ df -h /var
Filesystem  Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sdb1    50G   20G   30G  41% /var
o: The filesystem has run out of inodes
Right. Every file needs an inode. Millions of tiny files can use them all while space is left. df -i would show 100%.
The disk has bad sectors
Bad sectors show I/O errors in dmesg, not "No space left on device" next to 30 GB free.
The user has no write permission
That would say "Permission denied", not "No space left on device".
/var is mounted read-only
A read-only mount says "Read-only file system".

quiz.q: A server can ping 10.0.0.1, its gateway, and 8.8.8.8, but apt update fails with "Temporary failure in name resolution". Where should you look FIRST?
o: The DNS settings (/etc/resolv.conf or resolvectl status)
Right. Pinging IPs works, so the link and routing are fine. Only turning names into addresses is failing.
The default route
Pinging 8.8.8.8 works, so traffic already leaves the local network.
The firewall's HTTPS rules
A firewall block would cause a timeout or refusal, not a name resolution error.
The network interface driver
The interface works: the server reaches its gateway and the internet by IP.

quiz.q: Apache on a RHEL-family server returns 403 Forbidden for files moved from a home folder into /srv/www. The permissions are 644 and the folder is 755. What is the BEST next step?
o: Check the SELinux labels (ls -Z, ausearch -m avc), then fix them with semanage fcontext and restorecon
Right. Moved files keep their old home-folder label, which httpd isn't allowed to read. Relabel them; don't turn SELinux off.
chmod -R 777 /srv/www
The permissions already let Apache read. 777 adds risk and doesn't fix an SELinux denial.
setenforce 0
That turns off SELinux protection for the whole server to hide one labeling mistake.
Restart httpd
A restart doesn't change the files' labels, so the 403 comes right back.

quiz.q: Users say a file server is crawling. top shows a load average of 14.2 on 4 CPUs, with 3% us, 1% sy and 91% wa. What is the bottleneck?
o: Disk I/O
Right. wa is the time CPUs sit waiting on disk. Check which disk and process with iostat and iotop.
CPU
The CPUs are only 4% busy doing real work (us + sy). They're mostly waiting.
Not enough RAM
Memory pressure shows up as swap use and low available memory. Heavy swapping can raise wa, but the numbers given point straight at disk.
The network link
Network trouble doesn't show up as I/O wait in top. Check that with ip -s link or ss.

pbqs.title: Diagnose six server tickets
pbqs.scenario: Six Linux tickets came in overnight. Read each output and pick the cause. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.log:
$ curl -m 5 https://10.0.2.15
curl: (28) Connection timed out
# on the server:
$ ss -tlnp | grep 443
LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:443 users:(("nginx"))
$ firewall-cmd --list-services
ssh dhcpv6-client
items.why: nginx is listening on 443, but firewalld only allows ssh. Add the https service with --permanent and reload.

items.log:
$ systemctl status app
○ app.service - Unit app
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/app.service; disabled; preset: disabled)
     Active: inactive (dead)
items.why: The unit is fine but disabled, so it never starts at boot. systemctl enable --now app.

items.log:
$ touch /var/spool/mq/test
touch: cannot touch '/var/spool/mq/test': No space left on device
$ df -h /var | tail -1
/dev/sdb1  50G  21G  29G  42% /var
$ df -i /var | tail -1
/dev/sdb1  3.2M  3.2M  0  100% /var
items.why: Space is left but every inode is used. Find the folder with millions of small files and clean it up.

items.log:
$ ausearch -m avc -ts recent
type=AVC msg=audit(...): avc: denied { read } for pid=2211
 comm="httpd" name="index.html"
 scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0
 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0
items.why: The file kept its home-folder label (user_home_t) when it was moved. Relabel with restorecon so httpd can read it.

items.log:
$ ping -c1 10.0.0.1
1 packets transmitted, 1 received
$ dnf check-update
Curl error (6): Couldn't resolve host name
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.0.0.250
$ ping -c1 10.0.0.250
1 packets transmitted, 0 received
items.why: The network works by IP, but the only DNS server listed doesn't answer, so no names resolve.

items.log:
$ top
load average: 14.20, 13.87, 12.95
%Cpu(s):  3.1 us,  1.0 sy,  0.0 ni,  4.5 id, 91.4 wa
MiB Mem :  15890 total,   6120 free
items.why: 91% wa: the CPUs are waiting on disk. Use iostat and iotop to find the busy disk and process.

pbqs.title: Review these permissions
pbqs.scenario: You're running a hardening review on a Linux server. For each file, pick the risk and the fix. Some files are fine as they are.

rows.why: SUID on a root-owned program lets any user run it as root. Remove the bit.
Cron runs this file's jobs as root, and anyone can edit it. 644 lets only root write.
The t is the sticky bit: anyone can write, but only the owner can delete. That's how /tmp should be.
Every user can read the password hashes and try to crack them offline. Take away others' read.
Anyone could drop their own key into authorized_keys and log in as jdoe. sshd also refuses keys from a folder this open.
A private key readable only by its owner is exactly right.

pbqs.title: Run the right command
pbqs.scenario: Pick the command that does each task. Some options aren't used.

rows.req: Start nginx now and at every boot
rows.why: enable sets it to start at boot; --now also starts it right away.

rows.req: Make sure the old telnet service can never be started
rows.why: mask links the unit to /dev/null, so nothing can start it, not even as a dependency.

rows.req: You just edited a unit file. Make systemd see the change
rows.why: daemon-reload rereads unit files. Restart the service after it.

rows.req: Show nginx's log messages since the last boot
rows.why: -u picks the unit and -b limits it to this boot. -f would only follow new lines.

rows.req: Block jdoe from logging in, but keep the account
rows.why: usermod -L locks the password. userdel would remove the account.

rows.req: Run a backup script every day at 2:00 AM
rows.why: Cron fields are minute, hour, day, month, weekday. 0 2 means minute 0 of hour 2. 2 0 would be 12:02 AM.

rows.req: Set aside uncommitted work before switching branches
rows.why: git stash shelves the changes; reset --hard would delete them.
